warsangali-sultanate.t: A long-lived Somali sultanate on the Gulf of Aden coast, enriched by frankincense and later allied with the Dervish resistance.
warsangali-sultanate.o: According to tradition the Warsangali clan, of the Harti branch of the [[e:darod|Darod]], established a sultanate in the [[e:sanaag|Sanaag]] region of northern [[s:somalia|Somalia]] around 1298 under the Gerad dynasty. Its centre was the coastal town of [[e:las-khorey|Las Khorey]], with links inland to the highlands of the [[e:cal-madow|Cal Madow]] range.
warsangali-sultanate.r: The sultan, or gerad, ruled alongside clan elders according to [[e:somalis|Somali]] customary law and Islamic law. The economy rested on [[e:pastoralism|pastoralism]] and the export of frankincense, gum and livestock through [[e:las-khorey|Las Khorey]] to [[e:aden|Aden]] and the Arabian coast. Like its neighbours, the sultanate was a clan polity rather than a centralised state, and its early history comes mostly from oral tradition.
warsangali-sultanate.e: In 1886 the sultanate signed a protection treaty with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and became part of [[s:british-somaliland|British Somaliland]]. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] [[e:mohamoud-ali-shire|Mohamoud Ali Shire]] sided with the [[s:dervish-state|Dervish State]] and was exiled to the [[s:british-seychelles|Seychelles]] in 1920. The sultan's title survives as a traditional office in the [[e:sanaag|Sanaag]] region.

wassoulou-empire.t: The empire of Samori Toure, which fought French expansion in West Africa for nearly two decades with modern weapons and a disciplined army.
wassoulou-empire.o: [[e:samori-ture|Samori Toure]], a [[e:mandinka|Maninka]] trader turned soldier, built a following in the upper [[e:niger-river|Niger]] region from the 1860s, conquering small chiefdoms in the [[e:wassoulou|Wassoulou]] and Konyan areas. By 1878 he ruled a substantial state with its capital at [[e:bissandugu|Bissandugu]], and in 1884 he took the Muslim title almamy.
wassoulou-empire.r: Samori governed through provinces run by relatives and trusted commanders, with a standing army of sofa infantry. He bought repeating rifles in [[e:freetown|Freetown]], paid for with gold, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and slaves, and had local smiths copy them. He promoted [[e:islam|Islam]] and [[e:quran|Qur'anic]] schools. After clashes from 1882 and treaties in 1886 and 1887, he fought the French repeatedly, and in the 1890s moved his whole state east, to the lands of the [[s:kong-empire|Kong Empire]].
wassoulou-empire.e: In the east he destroyed [[e:kong-cote-divoire|Kong]] and fought the British and French. On 29 September 1898 the French captured him at Guelemou. Exiled to [[s:gabon-french-colony|Gabon]], he died in 1900, remembered across [[e:west-africa|West Africa]] as a hero of resistance.

western-ganga-dynasty.t: The Ganga kings of southern Karnataka, great patrons of Jainism, whose minister raised the colossal statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola.
western-ganga-dynasty.o: The Western Gangas established themselves in the 4th century in [[e:gangavadi|Gangavadi]], the southern [[e:karnataka|Karnataka]] plateau, as the [[s:pallava-dynasty|Pallava dynasty]]'s power waned. Their early capital was [[e:kolar|Kolar]], later moved to [[e:talakad|Talakad]] on the Kaveri. Tradition says the [[e:jainism|Jain]] teacher Simhanandi helped found the dynasty.
western-ganga-dynasty.r: [[e:durvinita|Durvinita]], an early king, was a scholar who translated works into [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]]. The Gangas often served as allies or feudatories of larger neighbours, the [[s:chalukyas-of-badami|Chalukyas of Badami]] and the [[s:rashtrakuta-dynasty|Rashtrakuta dynasty]], and [[e:butuga-ii|Butuga II]] fought for the Rashtrakutas against the [[s:chola-empire|Cholas]]. Their land grants supported [[e:jainism|Jain]] monasteries and [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] temples. Around 983 [[e:chavundaraya|Chavundaraya]], minister of [[e:rachamalla-iv|Rachamalla IV]], commissioned the 17-metre [[e:gommateshwara-statue|statue of Bahubali]] at [[e:shravanabelagola|Shravanabelagola]], and [[e:kannada|Kannada]] literature flourished.
western-ganga-dynasty.e: After the fall of the [[s:rashtrakuta-dynasty|Rashtrakutas]] the Gangas lost their protector. [[e:rajaraja-i|Rajaraja I]] of the [[s:chola-empire|Chola Empire]] captured [[e:talakad|Talakad]] around 1000, ending Ganga rule; [[e:gangavadi|Gangavadi]] later passed to the [[s:hoysala-empire|Hoysala Empire]].

wala-state.t: Kingdom of north-western Ghana centred on Wa, ruled by a Mole-Dagbani-linked dynasty alongside an influential Muslim community.
wala-state.o: Wala traditions describe the arrival in the 17th century of horsemen linked to the [[s:kingdom-of-dagbon|Dagbon]] and [[s:mamprugu|Mamprugu]] royal lines, who joined with Muslim [[e:wangara|Dyula]] traders and the local earth-priests to form a state around the town of Wa in the [[e:black-volta|Black Volta]] region.
wala-state.r: The Wa Na was chosen in rotation from several royal gates, while Muslim families held important offices and the earth-priests kept control of land rites. Wa was a stage on routes linking the [[e:niger-bend|Niger bend]] with the [[e:akan|Akan]] goldfields and [[s:hausa-kingdoms|Hausaland]], and its Friday mosques reflect a long tradition of Islamic scholarship.
wala-state.e: In the 1880s and 1890s Wa was ravaged by the slave-raiding armies of [[e:babatu|Babatu]] and [[e:samori-ture|Samori Ture]]. [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] took control in the late 1890s, and Wa became part of the [[s:northern-territories-of-the-gold-coast|Northern Territories of the Gold Coast]]. The Wa Na still reigns.

waalo.t: Wolof kingdom at the mouth of the Senegal river, squeezed for two centuries between Moorish emirates and the French at Saint-Louis.
waalo.o: Waalo occupied the lower [[e:senegal|Senegal]] valley and delta. [[e:wolof|Wolof]] tradition makes it the home of [[e:ndiadiane-ndiaye|Ndiadiane Ndiaye]], the legendary founder of the Wolof political order, and the kingdom is dated to the late 13th century. For much of its early history it was a province of the [[s:jolof-empire|Jolof Empire]], ruled by a king titled the [[e:brak|Brak]].
waalo.r: The [[e:brak|Brak]] was chosen from three royal maternal lineages by a council of [[e:prince-elector|electors]], and the queen mother and royal women held real power. After [[s:kingdom-of-jolof|Jolof]] broke up in 1549 Waalo was independent, trading slaves, gum arabic and grain with the French post at [[e:saint-louis-senegal|Saint-Louis]], founded in 1659, while suffering raids from the [[s:emirate-of-trarza|Trarza]] [[e:emirate|emirate]] to the north.
waalo.e: In 1819 or 1820 [[s:emirate-of-trarza|Trarza]] and Moorish raiders attacked the royal town of Nder, where the women of the court chose death by fire rather than capture. Under Queen [[e:ndatte-yalla-mbodj|Ndatte Yalla]] resistance continued, but the French governor [[e:louis-faidherbe|Faidherbe]] annexed Waalo in 1855 and it became part of [[s:french-senegal|French Senegal]].
